projects.title: An Interactive Food Chain Lesson
projects.subtitle: THE MEADOW HAS GONE QUIET
projects.description: The Meadow Has Gone Quiet — A Scenario-Based Safety eLearning Experience
projects.problem:
This project came out of an assignment with a deceptively simple brief: design an interactive lesson for young learners that teaches a foundational science concept through gamification rather than exposition. Food chains and energy flow are usually taught as a static diagram — sun, arrow, grass, arrow, rabbit — memorized and forgotten. My challenge was to turn that diagram into something a learner builds themselves, getting it wrong a few times along the way, because the wrong answers are where the real learning happens.

For a K-12 audience, that meant balancing playfulness against instructional rigor: it needed to feel like a game, but every interaction had to reinforce the underlying science, not just reward tapping the right icon.
projects.solution: The final product is a single-scenario, tap-to-sequence interactive lesson built in Genially: learners restore "the meadow's energy" by correctly ordering the trophic levels, receive scaffolded, concept-specific feedback on incorrect attempts, and finish with a fully visualized food chain plus a formal knowledge check. The design leans on game mechanics — progress tracking, a soft narrative goal, visual rewards — without ever letting the mechanic outrun the content; every tap is tied to a specific piece of the underlying science.
projects.results: This project was completed as part of a certification assignment rather than for a live client, so I don't have usage or assessment data to report here. What it demonstrates is my approach to designing for a young audience: using narrative framing and visible feedback loops to make an abstract system tangible, and treating incorrect answers as teaching moments rather than dead ends. It's a design pattern I'd extend to any lesson — regardless of age group — where the goal is for learners to internalize a process, not just recall a fact.
process: Rather than opening with vocabulary, I opened with a story problem: "The meadow has gone quiet. Something stopped the flow of energy. Can you restart it?" This reframes an abstract system (energy transfer through trophic levels) as a concrete, emotionally engaging puzzle — a technique I leaned on deliberately to lower the cognitive barrier to entry for younger learners.

Learners rebuild the food chain piece by piece — Energy Source → Producer → Primary Consumer → Secondary Consumer → Decomposer — with a visible progress tracker ("Energy Restored: 0/5" building to "5/5"). Each successful placement animates the energy visibly flowing through the meadow, giving learners an immediate, visual payoff tied directly to the concept, not just a generic "correct!" chime.

Wrong answers don't just say "incorrect" — they redirect with a targeted hint tied to the underlying logic: "Wrong! The fox needs something to hunt. Who comes before the fox, and what does it feed on? Also, don't forget to think about its ultimate source of energy." This was a deliberate choice: every wrong-answer state teaches the reasoning path back to the right answer instead of just flagging the error.

Rather than ending at the top predator (the intuitive stopping point for a young learner), I extended the chain to decomposers, framed as "the clean-up crew," to reinforce that energy flow is cyclical, not linear — nutrients return to the soil so producers can grow again.

The lesson closes with an embedded activity segment (true/false checks on energy flow) and a printable "Food Chains: Knowledge Check" worksheet with a word bank (Producer, Consumer, Decomposer, Energy Source), giving instructors a way to verify transfer of learning beyond the interactive portion.

I built supporting visual assets in Canva to maintain a consistent illustrated, storybook-like aesthetic throughout — reinforcing the meadow narrative rather than breaking it with mismatched stock imagery.

projects.title: Welcome Aboard: New Hire Orientation
projects.subtitle: Everything new team members need to hit the ground running
projects.description: This comprehensive onboarding course combines self-paced eLearning modules with interactive activities to help new hires understand company culture, policies, and their role responsibilities.
projects.overview: A comprehensive onboarding experience designed for a mid-size tech company, combining self-paced learning modules with interactive knowledge checks and real-world application activities.
projects.problem: The existing onboarding process relied on lengthy PDFs and live presentations, resulting in low engagement and inconsistent knowledge transfer across departments.
projects.solution: I redesigned the onboarding experience as a blended learning program, combining Articulate Rise modules for self-paced learning with Camtasia video walkthroughs for software training.
projects.results: New hire satisfaction scores increased by 35%, and time-to-productivity decreased by 2 weeks on average.
process: Interviewed stakeholders and new hires to identify pain points
Mapped learning objectives to measurable outcomes
Designed microlearning modules in Articulate Rise
Developed interactive job aids and quick-reference guides
Piloted with a cohort of 15 new hires and iterated

projects.title: Quick Reference: Customer Service Excellence
projects.subtitle: A visual guide to handling customer interactions with confidence
projects.description: This performance-based job aid provides customer service representatives with a visual, step-by-step guide to handling common customer scenarios, from greeting to resolution.
projects.overview: A visually engaging job aid designed for retail customer service representatives, providing quick-reference guidance for common customer interaction scenarios.
projects.problem: Customer service reps frequently consulted lengthy policy manuals during interactions, leading to longer resolution times and decreased customer satisfaction.
projects.solution: I created a visual, scannable job aid that distills key procedures into an intuitive flowchart format with clear decision points and scripted responses.
projects.results: Average call resolution time decreased by 20%, and customer satisfaction scores improved by 12%.
process: Observed customer service interactions and identified common scenarios
Interviewed top-performing reps for best practices
Designed visual flowchart with decision points
Created polished graphics in Canva and Adobe Illustrator
Tested with a pilot group and refined based on feedback
Distributed digitally and as printed desk reference
